newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG dropped German defence deal for mercenaries.
newsitem.headline: PNG dropped German defence deal for mercenaries.

text.p: Papua New Guinea only hired African mercenaries to crush an uprising on Bougainville island after abandoning plans for a US$24 million defence equipment and training contract with Germany, an inquiry was told on Tuesday.
Sacked PNG army chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok told the inquiry into last month's aborted mercenary operation the German contract was similar, but did not involve mercenaries.
"It would have been cheaper, but it was sustainable," said Singirok, who added he was forced by the government to drop the German negotiations in favour of the African mercenaries.

British-based military consultancy Sandline International signed a US$36 million contract with PNG in January to supply 70 African soldiers and weapons, including two Russian-made helicopter gunships, for an assault against Bougainville's secessionist rebels.
But Singirok led an army rebellion against the Sandline mercenaries in March and forced prime minister Sir Julius Chan to stand down pending an inquiry into the deal.
Singirok said a PNG defence force team, followed by a government mission, were sent to Germany in early 1996 to discuss a defence contract.

Under the proposal Germany would have issued PNG with a concessional five-year loan of US$21 million to pay for the bulk of the contract, with PNG picking up the rest. The contract would probably have infuriated Australia, which has tried to restrict arms sales to PNG.
Singirok said the German contract involved the training of PNG troops and the supply of equipment, but he did not say where the training would take place or what weapons would be bought.
"The contract would have been similar to the Sandline contract, except there are no mercenaries involved and that it would have been cheaper," Singirok said.
Singirok said he was involved in negotiations with a German government representative in Port Moresby in mid-1996 when he was forced by the PNG government to end the talks.
"The issue of Sandline came and overtook all the work done on the German contract, he said.

Singirok said he came under intense pressure from the PNG government, in particular defence minister Mathias Ijape who has also stepped aside, to accept the Sandline contract, despite personal misgivings about the use of mercenaries.
Singirok said that in a meeting in mid-February, Ijape told him that he could personally benefit from the mercenary deal.

"He said: 'Bro (brother), you can become a rich man if you engage this group'," said Singirok, who returned to the court a bag containing US$400,000 cash seized from the British mercenary commander Tim Spicer.
Singirok said that if he had made his objections public he would have simply been sacked and a defence chief favourable to the mercenary deal would have been appointed.
"I had reservations from day one, but I had to obey the ordered of the (defence) minister," Singirok said.
Singirok also said that Ijape had constantly talked about reopening Bougainville's giant Panguna copper mine with the assistance of an associated mercenary company in London.
Sandline chief executive Spicer, a retired British colonel who led the aborted mercenary mission, has denied his company wanted mining concessions on Bougainville.
However, a Sandline document signed by him and presented to the inquiry suggested a joint venture with the PNG government to run the Panguna mine once recaptured.
Illegal firearm charges against Spicer, who has been detained in Port Moresby for the past three weeks, were dropped on Monday evening, freeing the former Scots Guard to leave PNG.
